name: Amoxicillin
pediatricNote: WHO weight bands (per dose, every 12h): 3–<6kg 125mg; 6–<10kg 250mg; 10–<15kg 500mg; 15–<20kg 750mg; 20–<30kg 1000mg; ≥30kg adult dose
duration: 5 days (fast-breathing pneumonia: 3 days in low-HIV settings)
notes: Pediatric dose follows WHO 2014 revised pneumonia guidance (40mg/kg/dose twice daily) and the WHO AWaRe Antibiotic Book. Not a first-choice antibiotic for UTI or skin infections under AWaRe. Can take with or without food.

name: Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX)
pediatricNote: HIV prophylaxis (once daily): <6mo or <5kg 120mg; 6mo–5y or 5–15kg 240mg; 6–14y or 15–30kg 480mg; >14y or >30kg 960mg
notes: Pediatric treatment dose is total co-trimoxazole (4mg TMP/kg = 24mg co-trimoxazole/kg). HIV prophylaxis (WHO 2014): adults 960mg once daily, continued regardless of pregnancy stage; also reduces malaria in people with HIV. Not recommended by WHO for shigellosis (resistance). Caution in G6PD deficiency.

rules.message: Not for neonates under 4 weeks (kernicterus risk). HIV-exposed infants start co-trimoxazole prophylaxis at 4–6 weeks.

name: Metronidazole
notes: Use with caution in the 1st trimester of pregnancy (follow national formulary). C. difficile: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are preferred where available; metronidazole 500mg every 8h for 10 days is an alternative for non-severe disease only. Avoid alcohol during treatment and 48h after. Metallic taste is common.

rules.message: Pregnancy: use with caution in the 1st trimester (follow national formulary).

name: ORS (Oral Rehydration Salts)
adultDose: As much as wanted (about 200–400ml after each loose stool)
pediatricNote: Plan A (after each loose stool): < 2y 50–100ml; 2–10y 100–200ml; older: as much as wanted. Plan B: 75ml/kg over 4h, then reassess.
notes: WHO low-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L). 1 sachet + 1L clean water. Severe dehydration (Plan C): give IV fluids first; if IV is not possible, give ORS by nasogastric tube and refer urgently. Give ORS by mouth as soon as the patient can drink. In severe acute malnutrition use ReSoMal instead (except suspected cholera).

name: Zinc sulfate
adultDose: Not recommended by WHO for adults
notes: Give alongside ORS for all children under 5 with diarrhea. Not needed for children receiving zinc-fortified therapeutic foods (F-75, F-100, RUTF).

name: Vitamin A
adultDose: No routine supplementation for adults. For xerophthalmia or measles in adults, follow national guidance.
pediatricFreq: single dose (measles: day 1 & 2; eye signs: day 1, 2 & 14)
duration: Single dose (measles: 2 doses; eye signs of deficiency: 3 doses)
indications: SAM (only if therapeutic foods are not fortified)
contraindications: Pregnancy or possible pregnancy: never give a single dose > 25,000 IU (teratogenic)
notes: SAM (WHO 2013): no high-dose vitamin A if the child receives WHO-standard F-75, F-100 or RUTF. Give one age-based dose on admission only if foods are not fortified; repeat on day 2 and 14 only with eye signs or recent measles. Postpartum supplementation is not recommended by WHO.

rules.message: Pregnant or possibly pregnant: never give a high-dose capsule (> 25,000 IU). Maximum 10,000 IU/day or 25,000 IU/week (WHO 2011).

name: Mebendazole
notes: WHO 2017 preventive chemotherapy: 500mg single dose once or twice yearly depending on prevalence; pregnant women may be treated after the 1st trimester. Pinworm is usually treated with a repeat dose after 2 weeks. Can be crushed and mixed with food.

rules.message: Not for children under 1 year (WHO preventive chemotherapy starts at 12 months).

name: Artemether-lumefantrine (AL / Coartem)
pediatricNote: Tablets of 20/120mg: 5–<15kg: 1 tab; 15–<25kg: 2 tabs; 25–<35kg: 3 tabs; ≥35kg: 4 tabs — all × 6 doses at 0, 8, 24, 36, 48, 60h. With 40/240mg tablets, halve the tablet count.
notes: Preferred treatment in all trimesters of pregnancy, including the 1st trimester (WHO, Nov 2022). Infants < 5kg: use the dedicated infant formulation (artemether-lumefantrine 5/60mg dispersible, for 2–<5kg) — do not split older-child tablets. Must be taken with food — fat increases absorption. Complete the full course.

rules.message: Under 5 kg: use the infant formulation (artemether-lumefantrine 5/60mg dispersible, for 2–<5 kg) — do not use standard tablets.

name: Ciprofloxacin
pediatricNote: Shigellosis: 15mg/kg every 12h for 3 days. Cholera: 20mg/kg single dose (max 1g).
duration: Shigellosis: 3 days; cholera: single dose; typhoid: per local resistance
contraindications: Avoid in children unless benefit > risk
notes: Cholera (GTFCC 2022): doxycycline is first-line for all ages including pregnant women; ciprofloxacin or azithromycin are alternatives. Antibiotics only for eligible cholera patients (e.g. severe dehydration). Fluoroquinolone resistance in S. Typhi is widespread — check local data. Give 2h before or 4–6h after zinc, antacids or dairy.

rules.message: Pregnancy: use only if no safer alternative. For cholera, doxycycline or azithromycin are preferred (GTFCC 2022).

name: Ceftriaxone
pediatricNote: Severe pneumonia / sepsis: 80mg/kg once daily. Meningitis: 100mg/kg once daily or 50mg/kg every 12h (max 4g/day).
contraindications: Premature neonates up to 41 weeks postmenstrual age
notes: Pediatric dosing per WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children (2013). Meningitis needs the higher dose — the calculated 80mg/kg/2g cap applies to pneumonia/sepsis. Gonorrhea: WHO 2024 recommends 1g IM single dose. Reconstitute 1g in 3.5ml 1% lidocaine for IM (less pain; never IV). IV: dilute in 50–100ml NS over 30 min.

rules.message: Neonates need a different regimen: 50mg/kg every 12h if < 7 days old, 75mg/kg after 1 week (meningitis, with gentamicin). Contraindicated in premature neonates (up to 41 weeks postmenstrual age), neonatal jaundice, or with IV calcium-containing fluids — use cefotaxime instead.
